node.label: Theda Skocpol
node.date_label: States and Social Revolutions (1979) · Bringing the State Back In, co-edited (1985) · Protecting Soldiers and Mothers (1992) · Diminished Democracy (2003)
node.description: In States and Social Revolutions (1979), Theda Skocpol argues that revolutions require an explanation combining state structures, international pressures and class relations. Comparing France, Russia and China, she places states’ administrative and coercive organizations at the centre of the account rather than treating them as expressions of class interests. William H. Sewell Jr. praised the comparison but challenged its treatment of ideology; Skocpol acknowledged that her account had been too cursory while questioning his alternative conception of culture. Protecting Soldiers and Mothers (1992) shifted attention to American social policy, tracing veterans’ pensions and women’s organized reform. Linda Gordon disputed its handling of gender, and Skocpol challenged Gordon’s assessment of the scholarship. Marisa Chappell’s retrospective describes the book as influential for women’s and gender historians while identifying its limited treatment of race. Diminished Democracy (2003) examines the replacement of participatory associations by professionally managed civic organizations.
node.representative_figures_and_works: States and Social Revolutions: A Comparative Analysis of France, Russia, and China (1979); Vision and Method in Historical Sociology (edited, 1984); Bringing the State Back In (co-edited with Peter B. Evans and Dietrich Rueschemeyer, 1985); Protecting Soldiers and Mothers: The Political Origins of Social Policy in the United States (1992); Social Revolutions in the Modern World (1994); Diminished Democracy: From Membership to Management in American Civic Life (2003).
node.scope_note: Read selected primary passages in the 1985 state chapter and the coauthored 1990 French Revolution chapter, publisher openings of the Sewell exchange, selected Mead review passages, and publisher descriptions. Principal monographs, the original Contention exchange, and Chappell’s article body remain unread in full.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Mars Unshackled” (1990), Skocpol and Meyer Kestnbaum criticize Hunt’s Politics, Culture, and Class in the French Revolution (1984) for separating revolutionary politics from state centralization and international warfare.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Primary coauthored chapter, pp. 15–16, subsection An “Internalist” Interpretation: “Most problematic” identifies the separation. Joint argument; Hunt’s book unread in this inquiry.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Mars Unshackled” (1990), Skocpol and Meyer Kestnbaum explicitly compare her States and Social Revolutions (1979) with Huntington’s Political Order in Changing Societies (1968) on state centralization and popular mobilization.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Primary chapter, pp. 14–15: “Like Samuel Huntington.” A bounded comparison, not an asserted debt; Huntington’s book unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: As Mead recounts in 1994, Gordon’s “Response to Theda Skocpol” (1993) contests the generalized treatment of women and gender in the debate over Protecting Soldiers and Mothers (1992).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Mead, p. 304 and n. 15 (p. 308), quotes Gordon, Response, p. 188, distinguishing women, masculinities and variable gender systems. Original unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: As Mead recounts in 1994, Skocpol’s “Soldiers, Workers, and Mothers” (1993) challenges Gordon’s ranking of scholarship on gender and early American social policy.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Mead, pp. 304–305 and n. 16 (p. 308), reports Skocpol’s charge of an elitist “hierarchy” and reproduces her reply. Original unread; no blanket rejection of feminist history asserted.
proposed_edges.map_label: Disputing a hierarchy of gender scholarship

proposed_edges.relationship: States and Social Revolutions (1979) combines state organization, international pressures and agrarian class relations in a comparative explanation of revolutionary transformation.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Cambridge book description, Description section; publisher summary only, not a fresh full-book reading. Existing field roster and ideology-debate strand retained.

proposed_edges.relationship: Chappell’s 2018 retrospective identifies Protecting Soldiers and Mothers (1992) as a stimulus to women’s and gender historians’ study of state-building, while recording criticism of its maternalism and racial omissions.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Publisher abstract, sentences 2–5: “bring the state back in.” Reception is Chappell’s assessment; article body and Skocpol’s book unread in full.

proposed_edges.relationship: Protecting Soldiers and Mothers (1992) contributed to political history through Skocpol’s account of American state formation, emphasizing courts, patronage-based parties, federalism and federated civic organizations, as Robert C. Lieberman’s 2024 historiographical essay explains.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read the publisher’s open HTML section and bibliography. Lieberman explicitly identifies the institutional argument and its extension in subsequent research. American political development is mapped to the existing political-history field, whose description includes institutions and power. The 1992 book was not independently read.
proposed_edges.map_label: American state formation and social provision
